newsitem.title: THAILAND: Baht float may cause Thai budget revision - papers.
newsitem.headline: Baht float may cause Thai budget revision - papers.

text.p: Thailand may have to cut next year's budget to offset the revenue shortfall caused by the flotation of the baht, local newspapers reported on Saturday.

The newspapers quoted Deputy Finance Minister Chaturon Chaisaeng as saying the managed flotation will likely dent government earnings and prompt a readjustment of the 982 billion baht budget for the 1997/98 (October-September) fiscal year.
The readjustment will be carried out only after the baht stabilises, which is expected to take a couple of weeks, the Bangkok Post quoted Chaturon as saying.

When the budget passed its first reading late last month the exchange rate was about 25 baht per dollar, which made the budget equalivalent to about $39.3 billion. Since the government floated the baht last week the currency weakened to about 28.5 per dollar, reducing the budget to the equivalent of about $34.5 billion.

The Nation newspaper said tax officials have issued revised revenues projections that are about 90 billion baht below previous figures. Other officials predicted the cost of servicing the external debt would rise by six billion baht, the newspaper said.
Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh is due to map out an urgent response to the expected revenue shortfall at Monday's meeting of the Council of Economic Ministers, The Nation said.
The 1998 austerity budget, which proposes a four percent increase in spending year-on-year - the smallest rise in more than a decade - was hotly debated in parliament late last month.
During the debate, Chavalit's government was accused by the opposition of economic mismanagement.
Thailand's economy is currently going through its worst economic crisis since the mid-1980s, with growth dropping sharply, exports tumbling and the current account deficit widening.

Over the past few weeks the government has passed a series of drastic measures, including the baht float and the suspension of operations of 16 ailing finance firms, in order to try and bolster the ailing economy.
